rows.title: A rising coin, a mostly cash account

questions.prompt: What is the Bitcoin position worth after the rise?
questions.feedback: Multiply the $20,000 position by 1.10. The $2,000 gain belongs to the invested portion. A quoted percentage change describes the asset, not automatically every account that holds it.

questions.prompt: What is the return of the entire account in this case?
questions.feedback: Cash remains $80,000 and the position becomes $22,000, giving $102,000 total. Divide the $2,000 account gain by the original $100,000. That is 2%, before any costs excluded from this case.

questions.prompt: Which denominator gives the new Bitcoin allocation?
options: $102,000 total account value
$100,000 starting value
$22,000 position value
questions.feedback: The new weight is $22,000 divided by $102,000, approximately 21.57%. Using the original balance gives 22%, but that is not the current portfolio weight because total value changed.

questions.prompt: After the second 10% move down, what is the Bitcoin holding worth?
questions.feedback: Apply 0.90 to $22,000 to get $19,800. Equal opposite percentage moves use different bases, so they do not cancel and restore the original position value.

questions.prompt: What is the account worth after that second interval?
questions.feedback: Add unchanged $80,000 cash to the $19,800 holding. The account ends $200 below its original $100,000 despite the earlier asset rally.

questions.prompt: What is the account’s full-period return across both intervals?
questions.feedback: Divide the $200 loss by the original $100,000 account. The asset loses 1% across the sequence, but its original account weight was only 20%.

questions.prompt: At the $102,000 peak, what Bitcoin value equals a 20% target?
questions.feedback: Twenty percent of current $102,000 equity is $20,400. A $20,000 holding would be slightly below the target because the portfolio denominator has changed.

questions.prompt: In the separate fee-free rebalancing branch, how much Bitcoin value would be sold?
questions.feedback: Subtract the $20,400 target from the $22,000 holding. Selling $1,600 transfers value to cash and leaves equity unchanged when transaction fees are excluded.

questions.prompt: What is the decline from the $102,000 account peak to $99,800, approximately?
questions.feedback: The peak-to-current loss is $2,200. Divide by the $102,000 peak, rather than the original account balance, to obtain approximately 2.16%.

questions.prompt: Which statement distinguishes the two account branches accurately?
options: The price refresh automatically performs the rebalance
A 20% target guarantees a 20% account return
Rebalancing changes exposure through a separate order
questions.feedback: A price refresh only marks existing units. A rebalance changes units and cash through orders; choosing an allocation does not guarantee the resulting return.

rows.title: The unchanged-price round trip

questions.prompt: What is the fee on the $1,000 buy?
questions.feedback: A 0.1% fee is 0.001 times the trade value. Multiplying $1,000 by 0.001 gives $1. Converting a percentage to a decimal correctly matters before using any fee estimate.

questions.prompt: What is the net result of the flat-price round trip?
options: No gain or loss
A $1 gain
A $2 loss
questions.feedback: The buy debits $1,001 and the sale credits $999. Subtract the debit from the credit to obtain −$2. The asset made no price gain, but both fees affected the account.

questions.prompt: Would doubling the number of identical round trips remove that loss?
options: Yes; fees cancel each other
Yes; a flat price ensures break-even
No; it doubles these assumed fees
questions.feedback: Two identical round trips incur $4 of fees under these inputs. More activity alone does not create an edge. This case deliberately excludes other execution costs, so real-world costs could differ.

questions.prompt: What is total notional for one complete $1,000 buy and $1,000 sell?
questions.feedback: The buy and sale each count toward turnover, giving $2,000 total. Turnover measures traded notional, not equity earned or the final holding remaining.

questions.prompt: What net cash arrives from the unchanged-price $1,000 sale?
questions.feedback: Subtract the $1 sale fee from $1,000 gross proceeds. The buy fee is separate and must also be counted when reviewing the entire round trip.

questions.prompt: How many transactions occur across five of these round trips?
options: 5 transactions
20 transactions
10 transactions
questions.feedback: Each round trip includes one buy and one sell. Five completed pairs therefore contain ten fee-bearing transactions rather than only five.

questions.prompt: What total fee is charged across those five flat-price round trips?
questions.feedback: Ten transactions each cost $1, giving $10 total fees. The absence of price movement does not erase the accumulated costs of repeated activity.

questions.prompt: What combined gross price gain would cover those $10 fees exactly?
questions.feedback: Net result equals gross price gain minus costs. In this fixed-notional worksheet, a $10 gross gain covers the stated $10 charges without creating positive net profit.

questions.prompt: Does a fee-free hypothetical chart establish a fee-free execution ledger?
options: Yes; all flat charts imply zero costs
Yes; a plotted quote already includes every user fee
No; the transaction rules must also be checked
questions.feedback: A chart records prices, while an execution ledger records units, cash and applicable charges. The two must be combined before evaluating net performance.

questions.prompt: Which record would make this repeated-trading review reproducible?
options: Only the final asset symbol
Both transaction notionals and each fee
Only the count of profitable-looking charts
questions.feedback: Recording the buy and sell notionals and charges lets another reader reconstruct net cash. A chart or trade count alone does not identify the costs.

rows.title: A snapshot has an observation time

questions.prompt: How old is the stated observation at the 10:05 refresh?
options: Five hours
Three minutes
Zero minutes
questions.feedback: Subtract 10:02 from 10:05 to get three minutes. Refreshing a page does not necessarily obtain a new market observation; it can display a cached provider response with an older timestamp.

questions.prompt: Which timestamp best describes the age of the quote itself?
options: The time your account was created
The provider observation time
Only the page refresh time
questions.feedback: The observation timestamp belongs to the price data. The loading timestamp describes the interface request. Both can be useful, but substituting the latter can make an old observation appear newly priced.

questions.prompt: What should be checked before comparing the other website’s number?
options: Only the website’s font size
Matching asset, currency, time and methodology
Only which number is larger
questions.feedback: Two plausible prices can refer to different currencies, timestamps or market sources. An identifier and methodology check helps make the comparison meaningful; a visual difference alone does not establish an error.

questions.prompt: At the later 10:08 page visit, how old is the unchanged 10:02 observation?
options: Six minutes
One minute
Zero minutes
questions.feedback: Subtract the observation time from the viewing time. Fetching the same mark again at 10:08 does not reset its underlying age to zero.

questions.prompt: How old is the second page’s 10:07 observation at 10:08?
options: Six minutes
Eight minutes
One minute
questions.feedback: The second observation was recorded one minute before viewing. Its age differs from the first page even though both are inspected at the same time.

questions.prompt: Which stored field should remain unchanged when the same observation is served again?
options: The price silently converted into a forecast
The original observation timestamp
The original observation rewritten to 10:08
questions.feedback: A cache read should preserve the source observation’s timestamp. The response can have a new fetch time without suggesting the underlying price was observed again.

questions.prompt: Can a six-minute-old observation alone establish the price at 10:08?
options: No; it establishes a mark observed at 10:02
Yes; every successful fetch is a current quote
Yes; caching freezes the real market
questions.feedback: The mark describes the supplied observation time. Markets may move between observations, so a successful cached response is not proof of the current price.

questions.prompt: What identifier check should precede this timestamp comparison?
options: Matching font and display precision only
Matching website refresh animation
The same provider asset and quote currency
questions.feedback: Even simultaneous observations are not comparable if they identify different instruments or currencies. Resolve identity and units before attributing a difference to freshness.

questions.prompt: Which label communicates the first page’s data most accurately at 10:08?
options: Verified execution available at this price
Provider snapshot observed 10:02, fetched 10:08
Real-time price observed 10:08
questions.feedback: The label separates quote observation from page retrieval. It describes the available snapshot without promising current data or execution at a particular venue.

questions.prompt: What would strengthen a claim that one of these feeds is incorrect?
options: Matched-identity, matched-time evidence and provider methodology
A price difference with no timestamps
A faster refresh icon
questions.feedback: A time-aligned comparison can narrow alternative explanations such as different observation windows. Price differences alone do not establish which data source is wrong.

rows.title: An ETF can overlap a stock you own

questions.prompt: How much indirect A exposure is inside the ETF?
questions.feedback: Ten percent of the $8,000 ETF position is $800 under the assumed fixed weight. A fund holding can contain exposure to an asset already held directly, even though it appears as another row.

questions.prompt: What is the combined direct and indirect A exposure?
questions.feedback: Add the $2,000 direct holding and $800 look-through exposure. The resulting $2,800 is 28% of this $10,000 account. Counting the ETF as completely unrelated would miss the overlap.

questions.prompt: Does owning two rows guarantee broad diversification?
options: No; underlying exposures can overlap
Yes; row count is the diversification measure
Yes; any ETF eliminates company risk
questions.feedback: Diversification depends on what the instruments expose you to, not just how many names are displayed. A fund may hold many securities, but its overlap with direct positions can still increase concentration.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the account is directly invested in A?
questions.feedback: The direct $2,000 A position divided by $10,000 equity is 20%. Indirect exposure must be considered separately before computing the combined company sensitivity.

questions.prompt: What percentage of account equity is indirectly exposed to A through the ETF?
questions.feedback: The ETF’s $800 A slice divided by $10,000 account equity is 8%. The fund’s own 10% holding weight is not the whole account’s indirect exposure.

questions.prompt: What is total account weight dependent on A under the stated look-through method?
questions.feedback: Add 20% direct and 8% indirect company exposure. Counting the ETF as unrelated merely because it is a second row would miss the overlap.

questions.prompt: How much does the direct A holding lose in the 20% decline branch?
questions.feedback: Apply the selected 20% decline to the direct $2,000 position. The resulting $400 loss excludes the additional A exposure inside the ETF.

questions.prompt: How much does the ETF’s A slice lose in this branch?
questions.feedback: Apply 20% to the ETF’s $800 A exposure. Other constituents are assumed unchanged, so this $160 loss is the ETF’s supplied contribution from A.

questions.prompt: What is the combined account loss due to this A-only move?
questions.feedback: Add the $400 direct loss and $160 indirect loss. The $560 total is 5.6% of account equity under the fixed-weight, other-assets-unchanged assumptions.

questions.prompt: What change would invalidate treating this sensitivity as a complete account forecast?
options: Only the ETF name remaining the same
Only two rows being visible
Other fund holdings or weights also moving
questions.feedback: The worksheet isolates one company and freezes other inputs. Actual changes in constituents, weights or costs require a broader calculation and cannot be inferred from this isolated branch.

rows.title: A good process can have a losing outcome

questions.prompt: Does the winning result prove the undocumented process was better?
options: Yes; every profitable decision is well reasoned
Yes; evidence matters only after a loss
No; one outcome cannot establish that
questions.feedback: An outcome is one observation produced under uncertainty. It can be favorable despite a weak process or unfavorable despite careful reasoning. Assessing the pre-decision evidence avoids judging everything through hindsight.

questions.prompt: What should a process review examine first?
options: Only the final profit color
Only whether a friend agreed afterward
The information and rules available before acting
questions.feedback: Review the dated thesis, exposure and decision criteria before adding later information. That preserves a fair account of what could reasonably have been considered and makes later changes to the thesis visible.

questions.prompt: What would help compare the methods over time?
options: Deleting the losing decision
Calling either method certain after one result
Consistent prospective records across more decisions
questions.feedback: A complete sequence of records can reveal repeated weaknesses or strengths better than a selected result. It still needs context and uncertainty; prospective documentation reduces retrospective storytelling and omitted failures.

questions.prompt: How many of the three defined documentation items did A record?
options: Zero
Three
One
questions.feedback: The case explicitly records evidence, exposure and a review condition for A. Counting those items measures documentation completeness under this narrow worksheet definition.

questions.prompt: How many of those defined documentation items did B record?
options: Zero
Three
One
questions.feedback: The case says B skipped the listed steps. That creates a documentation gap even though B’s one supplied outcome happened to be profitable.

questions.prompt: What outcome difference separates B’s +$50 from A’s −$50?
questions.feedback: Subtract −$50 from +$50 to obtain a $100 gap. This single dollar comparison describes outcomes without establishing which process is repeatable.

questions.prompt: Does A’s complete checklist prove the next decision will win?
options: Yes; a review condition eliminates uncertainty
No; documentation is not a profit guarantee
Yes; all recorded processes are profitable
questions.feedback: A documented process can make assumptions reviewable, but the supplied checklist does not remove uncertainty or validate future returns.

questions.prompt: Which record helps assess whether each learner followed their stated plan?
options: The original dated plan and the actual actions
Only the final profit number
Only the winner’s username
questions.feedback: Comparing a plan written before the outcome with the subsequent actions distinguishes adherence from a story reconstructed after the result.

questions.prompt: What would make a repeated comparison more informative?
options: Selecting only the best decision from each learner
Changing the checklist to fit each outcome
Consistent inclusion rules, comparable exposure and costs
questions.feedback: Comparable records and predefined inclusion reduce selective interpretation. Exposure and costs affect outcomes, so a fair comparison requires more than repeating profit headlines.

questions.prompt: What feedback matches A’s single losing case without overclaiming?
options: The loss proves A should double the next position
The documented steps can be reviewed separately from the loss
The loss proves all three steps were useless
questions.feedback: The case permits a review of evidence, exposure and conditions independently of one outcome. It does not justify discarding the process or increasing risk automatically.

rows.title: Two unequal positions fall together

questions.prompt: How much does the stock position lose?
questions.feedback: The loss is $30,000 multiplied by 0.05, or $1,500. A price move must be applied to the dollars held in that asset; it is not applied to cash or to another position.

questions.prompt: What is the combined account loss?
questions.feedback: The crypto loses $10,000 × 20% = $2,000. Add the $1,500 stock loss to obtain $3,500. The account becomes $96,500, so its return is −3.5% under the stated assumptions.

questions.prompt: Why is a simple average of −5% and −20% unsuitable here?
options: Cash must lose 12.5% too
Losses cannot be added
The positions have different dollar weights
questions.feedback: A simple average assumes equal exposure to the two assets and omits cash. Dollar-weighted changes preserve the different position sizes. Neither asset volatility nor the number of holdings alone supplies the missing weights.

questions.prompt: How much does the crypto holding lose in the first interval?
questions.feedback: Twenty percent of the $10,000 crypto position is $2,000. Applying that percentage to the stock position or the whole account would use the wrong exposure.

questions.prompt: What is total equity immediately after both initial declines?
questions.feedback: The stock becomes $28,500 and crypto becomes $8,000. Add $60,000 cash to obtain $96,500, a $3,500 account loss.

questions.prompt: What contribution does the stock loss make to starting-account return?
options: −5 percentage points
−30 percentage points
−1.5 percentage points
questions.feedback: The stock loses $1,500 on a $100,000 starting account. Its own return is −5%, but its contribution to whole-account return is −1.5 percentage points.

questions.prompt: What is the stock value after its separate 5% rebound?
questions.feedback: Apply 1.05 to $28,500, giving $29,925. The rebound starts from a smaller base than the original decline and therefore does not fully reverse it.

questions.prompt: What is the crypto value after its separate 20% rebound?
questions.feedback: Multiply the reduced $8,000 position by 1.20. The $1,600 rebound is smaller than the earlier $2,000 loss because the percentage denominator changed.

questions.prompt: What is final account equity after both stated rebounds?
questions.feedback: Add $60,000 cash, $29,925 stock and $9,600 crypto. The account is still $475 below its original value despite both holdings’ positive second intervals.

questions.prompt: Which comparison describes the initial dollar loss contributions correctly?
options: Both lost equally because both prices fell
Crypto lost more dollars despite the smaller position
Stock lost more because its position was larger
questions.feedback: Crypto lost $2,000 and stock lost $1,500. Dollar impact depends on position size and percentage move together, rather than either one considered alone.

rows.title: A sale fee uses the exit value

questions.prompt: What is the sale fee under the stated rule?
questions.feedback: Multiply the $2,200 exit notional by 0.001. That gives $2.20. A fee on the transaction’s whole value differs from a tax or charge calculated only on profit.

questions.prompt: What net sale proceeds reach cash?
questions.feedback: Subtract the $2.20 sale fee from $2,200 gross proceeds. The $2,197.80 cash credit contains original capital and gain. It should not all be reported as profit.

questions.prompt: What is the net gain after the $2 buy fee and sale fee?
questions.feedback: The original cash debit was $2,002. Compare it with $2,197.80 net proceeds to get $195.80. Both fee bases are their respective trade values, and each fee is counted once.

questions.prompt: What initial cash outlay includes the $2,000 purchase and its fee?
questions.feedback: The purchase fee is $2,000 times 0.001, or $2. Add it to the purchase notional to obtain the full $2,002 entry debit.

questions.prompt: What gross price gain occurs at the $2,200 exit before any fees?
questions.feedback: Subtract original $2,000 purchase notional from $2,200 sale notional. This price-only gain has not yet accounted for either transaction charge.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of entry and exit fees in the $2,200 branch?
questions.feedback: The entry charge is $2 and the exit charge is $2.20. Add both to obtain $4.20 total, rather than counting only the latest transaction.

questions.prompt: What is net return on the $2,002 initial outlay, approximately?
questions.feedback: Divide the $195.80 net gain by $2,002 total entry debit. The denominator includes the buy fee because this comparison uses actual initial cash spent.

questions.prompt: In the separate $1,800 exit branch, what fee applies to the sale?
questions.feedback: Charge 0.1% to the actual $1,800 exit value. The fee is neither based on the original purchase nor only on the position’s $200 loss.

questions.prompt: In that $1,800 branch, what is the net loss including both fees?
questions.feedback: Net proceeds are $1,798.20 compared with $2,002 initial outlay. Their difference is a $203.80 loss, including the entry and exit fees.

questions.prompt: Why must the two alternative exit branches be kept separate?
options: One position cannot be sold in full twice without another purchase
Both branches automatically occur on refresh
The fee changes the number of holdings into two
questions.feedback: Each branch imagines a different full-sale price for the same starting holding. Combining both as actual proceeds would double-count quantity and cash.

rows.title: An aggregate is not one exchange’s last trade

questions.prompt: Does the $101 reference prove a trade occurred at exactly $101?
options: No; a reference can combine observations
Yes; every aggregate is a last trade
Yes; a midpoint is always executable
questions.feedback: An aggregate can summarize multiple market observations without being the price of a particular transaction. To describe a last trade, you need the actual venue, transaction and timestamp rather than only a reference figure.

questions.prompt: Can you recover the provider’s weighting method from these numbers alone?
options: No; methodology and input weights are missing
Yes; all aggregates are equal-weight averages
Yes; the larger venue price has full weight
questions.feedback: The stated reference happens to lie between the two inputs, but that does not reveal weighting, filtering or source coverage. Consult the methodology instead of inventing an algorithm from a single result.

questions.prompt: What does the simulator’s mark establish?
options: A valuation input for the paper account
A reserved real exchange fill
A guaranteed price for unlimited quantity
questions.feedback: A mark supports simulated valuation under the product’s rules. Real execution depends on an actual venue and available liquidity. Treat the provider number as a reference rather than a promise that money can be exchanged at that price.

questions.prompt: What reference does equal weighting of the two venue prices produce?
questions.feedback: Average the two supplied prices with equal weights: half of $100 plus half of $102 is $101. This matches the reported reference under one possible method.

questions.prompt: What reference results from 75% A and 25% B weights?
questions.feedback: Multiply $100 by 0.75 and $102 by 0.25, then add $75 and $25.50. The resulting $100.50 shows how different weights alter an aggregate.

questions.prompt: Does matching the equal-weight calculation prove the provider used that method?
options: No; several methods or inputs could produce $101
Yes; one arithmetic match proves the entire methodology
Yes; every aggregate must use equal weights
questions.feedback: A numerical match does not uniquely identify how a provider produced its reference. Additional observations or the published method are needed to establish the process.

questions.prompt: What is venue B’s price premium over venue A in percentage terms?
questions.feedback: Divide the $2 difference by venue A’s $100 price. The 2% relative gap should be labelled with its comparison base rather than treated as an account return.

questions.prompt: Does a calculated $100.50 reference imply a venue trade at that exact price?
options: Yes; it proves A’s $100 trade never occurred
No; a weighted reference can lie between venue observations
Yes; every reference is a recorded transaction
questions.feedback: A calculation can combine separate observations into a new reference value. That reference is not automatically evidence of an executed trade at the calculated price.

questions.prompt: Which additional data would be necessary to assess immediate execution?
options: Current venue bids, asks and relevant execution constraints
Only the aggregate reference
Only the arithmetic midpoint
questions.feedback: Execution depends on available orders and venue conditions. A reference price alone does not establish a bid or ask at which the user can actually transact.

questions.prompt: Which report keeps the hypothetical aggregation methods honest?
options: Attribute both to the provider as facts
Call the larger reference a guaranteed sale price
Label both weight choices as conceptual alternatives
questions.feedback: The case supplies alternative worksheet weights, not verified provider rules. Clear labels prevent a mathematical example from turning into an unsupported methodology claim.

rows.title: Correlation can change when you need it

questions.prompt: Does three earlier observations establish a permanent correlation?
options: Yes; three is always enough
Yes; opposite moves guarantee independence
No; the sample and period are limited
questions.feedback: Correlation is a sample-dependent statistic, not a fixed contract between assets. Three observations supply very little evidence, and a relationship estimated in one period may not hold in another.

questions.prompt: Can low past correlation guarantee no simultaneous losses?
options: Yes; simultaneous losses violate the definition
Yes; one asset must rise every day
No; individual intervals can still move together
questions.feedback: A low aggregate relationship can coexist with particular intervals where both assets fall. Correlation does not promise a hedge on every date, and changing conditions can alter the estimated relationship.

questions.prompt: What is the better way to describe the earlier evidence?
options: A guaranteed hedge
Proof of market-neutral profits
A limited historical pattern, with its sample stated
questions.feedback: Specify the period, observations and method used. Avoid upgrading a historical estimate into a guarantee. Even a designed hedge can retain mismatch, liquidity and cost risks beyond the correlation statistic.

questions.prompt: In how many of the four supplied observations do the assets move in opposite directions?
options: One observation
Three observations
Four observations
questions.feedback: The first three pairs have opposite signs while the fourth has two negative signs. Counting directions describes this sample without establishing a stable correlation coefficient.

questions.prompt: In the fourth observation, how much does a $1,000 A holding lose?
questions.feedback: Apply A’s selected 3% decline to $1,000 exposure. The $30 loss is a dollar contribution for this one observation, not the asset’s permanent risk.

questions.prompt: In that fourth observation, how much does a $1,000 B holding lose?
questions.feedback: Apply B’s selected 4% decline to $1,000. Its $40 loss joins the A loss rather than offsetting it in this particular same-direction observation.

questions.prompt: What is the combined fourth-observation loss on the equal-dollar holdings?
questions.feedback: Add $30 A loss and $40 B loss. Equal notionals do not force opposing performance when both supplied asset moves are negative.

questions.prompt: What return does that combined $2,000 position show for the fourth observation?
questions.feedback: Divide the $70 loss by the combined $2,000 starting value. Adding the two asset percentage declines without weighting would overstate the portfolio percentage.

questions.prompt: Do these direction counts alone supply a reliable long-run correlation estimate?
options: Yes; three opposite pairs guarantee permanent negative correlation
Yes; one same-direction pair proves permanent positive correlation
No; magnitudes, a suitable sample and method matter
questions.feedback: A small selected sample and sign counts cannot establish a durable statistical relationship. A defined method and broader representative observations are needed.

questions.prompt: Which statement is supported without overstating the evidence?
options: The fourth observation could not occur
Opposite earlier moves did not prevent a simultaneous loss in the fourth case
Diversification never helps
questions.feedback: The supplied pairs demonstrate that an earlier pattern did not hold in one later observation. They do not settle all diversification outcomes or future relationships.

rows.title: Write the thesis before the price moves

questions.prompt: What is the observed price change in this case?
questions.feedback: The $4 increase divided by the $40 starting price is 10%. That observed return is separate from why the learner acted and does not validate a reason invented after the movement.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with replacing the original reason after the rise?
options: It makes the report a proven cause
It prevents a fair test of the original hypothesis
It improves the historical evidence
questions.feedback: A rewritten explanation can make outcomes look more predictable than they were. Preserve the original thesis and add new information as a dated update rather than silently changing what the decision supposedly tested.

questions.prompt: What should a useful pre-decision note contain?
options: Only the hoped-for profit
Evidence, uncertainty and a review condition
A certainty claim about the next quote
questions.feedback: A brief note can state the observable evidence, alternative explanations and what would prompt reconsideration. It creates a reviewable process without pretending a future price is known.

questions.prompt: What notional was invested in the ten units at $40?
questions.feedback: Ten units multiplied by the original $40 quote gives $400 before fees. This is the invested notional, not the total size of an unspecified account.

questions.prompt: What is the later ten-unit holding worth at $44?
questions.feedback: Multiply ten unchanged units by the later $44 mark. The $440 value can be verified without accepting any particular explanation of the price increase.

questions.prompt: What is the holding’s gross dollar gain?
questions.feedback: Subtract $400 original notional from $440 marked value. Ten units translate the $4 per-unit price move into a $40 position gain.

questions.prompt: What is the quote’s return from $40 to $44?
questions.feedback: Divide the $4 quote increase by the $40 starting quote. This 10% gross asset return does not establish how much an entire account earned after costs.

questions.prompt: How should the later report be recorded without changing the original thesis?
options: As proof the original note always mentioned it
By deleting the chart-pattern reason
As dated new evidence beside the original note
questions.feedback: A dated addition preserves which evidence was available when the decision occurred. Overwriting the entry note hides the hypothesis actually tested.

questions.prompt: Does the $40 gain prove the later report caused the price move?
options: Yes; journals determine market prices
No; the case supplies no causal test
Yes; every positive result validates the latest story
questions.feedback: The arithmetic establishes a gain but not its cause. Attribution requires evidence connecting the event and price response beyond an after-the-fact explanation.

questions.prompt: What comparison would best reveal hindsight rewriting?
options: The original note against the later revised explanation
Only the final green return badge
Only another user’s account rank
questions.feedback: A preserved original record exposes which reasons changed after the outcome. This comparison supports process learning without requiring a confident market forecast.

rows.title: Cash after a fee-paying buy

questions.prompt: What is the total cash debit for this purchase?
questions.feedback: Twenty shares at $100 have a $2,000 notional value. The fee is $2,000 × 0.001 = $2, so cash falls by $2,002. Counting only share cost would leave the cash ledger overstated.

questions.prompt: What cash remains after that debit?
questions.feedback: Subtract the full $2,002 debit from $10,000. The resulting $7,998 cash plus $2,000 of shares equals $9,998 in equity at the unchanged mark; the $2 difference is the fee.

questions.prompt: Is the unchanged quote enough to keep total equity at $10,000?
options: No; equity is $7,998
No; equity is $9,998 after the fee
Yes; fees become holdings
questions.feedback: An unchanged asset price does not refund transaction costs. The marked holding still has $2,000 of value, but $2 has left cash. Equity includes cash and holdings, not the cash balance alone.

questions.prompt: What purchase fee is included in the original $2,002 debit?
questions.feedback: Convert 0.1% to 0.001 and multiply by the $2,000 notional. The $2 charge is an expense, not additional value held as shares.

questions.prompt: How many shares are owned immediately after this fee-paying purchase?
options: 20.02 shares
19.98 shares
20 shares
questions.feedback: The order buys exactly 20 shares and charges its fee separately in cash. A cash fee affects equity but does not silently alter the order quantity.

questions.prompt: At the later $110 quote, what is the position’s marked value?
questions.feedback: Twenty shares multiplied by $110 gives $2,200. Purchase fees affect net performance, but are not added to the current units-times-quote valuation.

questions.prompt: What exit fee applies to the $2,200 sale?
questions.feedback: Multiply the $2,200 sale notional by 0.001. Reusing the original $2 purchase fee would understate the charge on this larger exit value.

questions.prompt: What is final cash after selling all 20 shares?
questions.feedback: Add $2,197.80 net sale proceeds to $7,998 remaining cash. Both fees reduce the final balance below the amount implied by the gross $200 price gain.

questions.prompt: What is net account gain across the complete purchase and sale?
questions.feedback: Subtract original $10,000 cash from the $10,195.80 final balance. The $200 gross price gain is reduced by $2 entry and $2.20 exit fees.

questions.prompt: What is net return measured against the original account equity?
questions.feedback: Divide the $195.80 net gain by $10,000 starting equity. The share quote rose 10%, but only part of the account was invested and fees reduced the gain.

rows.title: An affordable quantity still needs fee room

questions.prompt: What would ten units cost including the fee?
questions.feedback: Ten units have a $1,000 notional, and 0.1% adds $1. The total exceeds available cash. A displayed balance that exactly matches notional does not leave room for a fee.

questions.prompt: Which stated whole-unit alternative fits the cash balance?
options: Nine units, costing $900.90
Ten units, costing $1,001
Eleven units, costing $1,101.10
questions.feedback: Nine units cost $900 plus $0.90 fee, or $900.90. The remaining $99.10 is cash. Checking the full debit is more reliable than checking notional alone.

questions.prompt: What should an insufficient-cash message lead you to inspect first?
options: Quantity, current quote and the total debit
Whether the asset must rise tomorrow
Whether fees can be ignored in a simulator
questions.feedback: Affordability depends on the current price, requested quantity and applicable costs. It is an execution constraint, not a signal about direction. Reducing a quantity should follow a budget check rather than a forecast.

questions.prompt: What is the fee on the attempted ten-unit $1,000 purchase?
questions.feedback: Multiply $1,000 notional by 0.001 to obtain a $1 fee. Spending the entire cash balance on notional leaves no room for this separate charge.

questions.prompt: What cash shortfall does the ten-unit order create?
questions.feedback: Total debit would be $1,001 against only $1,000 available. The $1 difference explains the failure without implying any missing price data.

questions.prompt: What does nine units cost including the stated fee?
questions.feedback: Nine units at $100 give $900 notional and a $0.90 fee. The total is $900.90, so this whole-unit alternative fits the cash balance.

questions.prompt: How much cash remains after the nine-unit purchase?
questions.feedback: Subtract the $900.90 debit from $1,000 cash. The remaining $99.10 accounts for both the holding’s purchase value and its transaction fee.

questions.prompt: What is the fee-inclusive cost per unit at this unchanged quote?
questions.feedback: Apply the 1.001 purchase-cost multiplier to $100 per unit. This $100.10 is cash spent per unit under the fee rule, not the asset’s new market quote.

questions.prompt: Without rounding constraints, what quantity just fits $1,000, approximately?
options: 9.99001 units
10 units
9.9 units
questions.feedback: Divide $1,000 by $100 times 1.001. Actual execution precision may require rounding this mathematical upper bound downward so the debit cannot exceed available cash.

questions.prompt: Which action addresses the stated insufficient-cash cause?
options: Repeatedly refresh until cash increases
Treat the fee as extra shares
Reduce quantity to leave room for the fee
questions.feedback: Adjusting quantity changes notional and its proportional fee. Refreshing a page does not create cash, and the fee does not add a holding.

rows.title: Currency mismatch looks like a price error

questions.prompt: What is €92 expressed in dollars at the stated exchange rate?
questions.feedback: Multiply €92 by $1.10 per euro to get $101.20. The currency units matter: dividing by 1.10 would use the opposite conversion and answer a different question.

questions.prompt: What dollar difference separates the converted quote from $100?
questions.feedback: The converted €92 quote is $101.20, so it is $1.20 above $100. Comparing the raw 92 and 100 without currency labels would suggest an $8 gap that is not this common-unit difference.

questions.prompt: What remains necessary for a reliable cross-site comparison?
options: A rule that the lower number is correct
Ignoring conversion because both are prices
Matched timestamps and source definitions
questions.feedback: Currency conversion resolves one mismatch only. Different observation times, venue inputs or asset identifiers can still affect the comparison. A fair audit records these fields rather than declaring accuracy from one converted pair.

questions.prompt: At $1.10 per euro, what is the $100 quote worth in euros, approximately?
questions.feedback: Divide $100 by $1.10 per euro. The euro value is approximately €90.91; multiplying instead would reverse the conversion direction.

questions.prompt: At the original rate, what percentage premium does the €92 quote have over $100?
questions.feedback: The euro quote converts to $101.20, a $1.20 premium. Divide that gap by the $100 comparison price to obtain 1.2%.

questions.prompt: In the separate $1.08-per-euro branch, what is €92 in dollars?
questions.feedback: Multiply €92 by $1.08 per euro to obtain $99.36. This changes the converted value while the asset’s euro quote remains exactly the same.

questions.prompt: In that alternative-rate branch, how does the converted quote compare with $100?
options: It is exactly equal
It is $0.64 lower
It is $1.20 higher
questions.feedback: Subtract $99.36 from $100 to obtain a $0.64 discount. The direction of the cross-currency comparison changed solely because the assumed exchange rate changed.

questions.prompt: What dollar-per-euro rate would make €92 equal $100, approximately?
options: $1.08696 per euro
$0.92 per euro
$1.20 per euro
questions.feedback: Solve 92 times the conversion rate equal to 100. Dividing 100 by 92 gives approximately 1.08696 dollars per euro.

questions.prompt: Can changing the conversion rate prove the underlying euro asset price changed?
options: Yes; every dollar conversion change is an asset trade
Yes; conversion automatically changes units owned
No; the euro quote was held fixed in this branch
questions.feedback: The worksheet explicitly keeps €92 unchanged. Its dollar expression changes with the currency rate, without proving a new asset quote or any transaction.

questions.prompt: Which record makes the price comparison reproducible across currencies?
options: Only the chosen currency symbol
Both asset quotes, their times and the conversion rate used
Only the larger displayed number
questions.feedback: A reader needs values, units, observation times and the applied rate to reconstruct the comparison. Displayed numbers alone omit important conversion assumptions.

rows.title: A planned payoff ratio is not a realized result

questions.prompt: What gross total do four full winners contribute?
questions.feedback: Four winners times $300 each equal $1,200. This assumes every listed winner realizes the entire planned payoff. An intended target alone does not establish what a position actually returns.

questions.prompt: What is the net sample result after six full losses, before costs?
questions.feedback: Six losses total $600. Subtract $600 from the $1,200 gains to obtain a $600 positive sample result. It is a calculation for these exact outcomes, not proof that future attempts will match them.

questions.prompt: What would invalidate using this sample as a general profit promise?
options: Nothing; the planned ratio ensures profit
Different realized payoffs, outcomes or costs
Only a different chart color
questions.feedback: Actual win frequency, average realized gains, average losses and costs determine the result. Exits may differ from planned thresholds. A stated risk-to-reward ratio is not sufficient evidence of a profitable strategy.

questions.prompt: What is the recorded win rate across the ten original attempts?
questions.feedback: Four winning attempts divided by ten total attempts gives 40%. Win rate is a count-based measure and does not describe the size of each outcome.

questions.prompt: What gross loss do the six losing attempts contribute?
questions.feedback: Six losses of $100 each total $600. This loss must be subtracted from the winners’ $1,200 contribution in the original fixed-payoff sample.

questions.prompt: What is original average gross result per attempt?
questions.feedback: The original $600 gross sample gain divided by ten attempts is $60 each on average. It is a description of the sample rather than a forecast.

questions.prompt: With winners reduced to $200, what is the alternative gross sample gain?
questions.feedback: Four $200 winners contribute $800, and six $100 losses total $600. Subtract to obtain a $200 gross result in this separate branch.

questions.prompt: What total cost applies at $5 per attempt across ten attempts?
questions.feedback: Ten attempts each incur the specified $5 charge, giving $50 total. This conceptual fixed cost is separate from TradeHQ’s notional-based transaction fee.

questions.prompt: What net result remains in the $200-winner branch after those costs?
questions.feedback: Reduce the alternative $200 gross result by $50 costs. Changing realized winner size materially changes the sample outcome despite the same 40% win count.

questions.prompt: Why can’t the original planned payoff ratio guarantee the alternative result?
options: Realized exits and costs can differ from planned amounts
Every planned ratio executes automatically
A 40% win rate fixes all dollar results
questions.feedback: A plan specifies intended conditions, while actual outcomes determine realized profit. The alternative branch demonstrates that the same count can produce different net results.

rows.title: The old high is a reference, not a promise

questions.prompt: What is the decline from $200 to $120?
questions.feedback: The decline is $80 divided by the original $200, or 40%. This measures a past price change. It does not show that the current asset is undervalued or that the earlier high was justified.

questions.prompt: What rise from $120 would restore $200, approximately?
questions.feedback: The required $80 gain is divided by the current $120 base, giving approximately 66.67%. A 40% rebound would not undo a 40% loss because it applies to a smaller base.

questions.prompt: What conclusion does the earlier high alone support?
options: Only that the asset had a higher quoted price before
A guaranteed return to $200
A verified current bargain
questions.feedback: A historical price can anchor expectations without supplying present valuation evidence. Investigate current conditions and alternative outcomes instead of treating a prior high as an entitlement or an inevitable destination.

questions.prompt: What is the ten-unit position’s entry notional at $120?
questions.feedback: Ten units multiplied by $120 gives $1,200 before fees. The historic $200 high does not change the amount spent at the stated entry.

questions.prompt: At the separate $150 mark, what is the ten-unit position worth?
questions.feedback: Ten units times $150 gives $1,500. This selected branch is a calculation of marked value rather than a forecast that the asset will reach that quote.

questions.prompt: What is the return from the $120 entry to the $150 branch?
questions.feedback: Divide the $30 quote rise by the $120 entry. The 25% return uses the entry as base, not the older $200 high.

questions.prompt: At the separate $100 branch, what is the return from $120, approximately?
questions.feedback: The $20 decline divided by $120 is approximately −16.67%. Percentages differ when the reference base differs, even with similar dollar moves.

questions.prompt: How much must the ten-unit position gain to rise from $1,200 to the old-high value?
questions.feedback: Ten units at $200 would be $2,000. Subtract $1,200 current-entry value to obtain an $800 recovery gain for this specific quantity.

questions.prompt: Would calling $120 “40% off” establish an independently verified fair value?
options: No; it only compares the quote with an old high
Yes; the old high guarantees a bargain
Yes; all historical highs are fair-value estimates
questions.feedback: The 40% decline is a reference calculation. Without relevant valuation evidence, it cannot establish fair value or the likelihood of returning to the earlier quote.

questions.prompt: Which question would extend the analysis beyond anchoring to the high?
options: How can the old high be treated as certain?
How many times can the old high be repeated?
What current evidence supports the valuation assumptions?
questions.feedback: A current evidence-based valuation review addresses assumptions and uncertainty. Repeating a historic price alone does not supply missing information about value or future outcomes.

rows.title: Selling half is not selling the gain

questions.prompt: How much gross cash arrives from the five-share sale?
questions.feedback: Five shares multiplied by the $100 sale price gives $500 proceeds. Proceeds include both recovery of original capital and profit; they are not the same thing as the realized gain.

questions.prompt: What is the gross realized gain on those five shares?
questions.feedback: The sold shares cost 5 × $80 = $400. Subtract this cost from $500 proceeds for a $100 gross realized gain. The other $100 price gain remains attached to the five unsold shares.

questions.prompt: How should a net-return review handle transaction fees?
options: Include applicable buy and sell fees once
Ignore fees because some shares remain
Subtract the full sale proceeds
questions.feedback: Net performance includes relevant transaction expenses. Record which fee belongs to which calculation and avoid double counting. Gross realized gain, remaining unrealized gain and net account return answer different questions.

questions.prompt: What original cost belongs to the five shares sold?
questions.feedback: Five shares bought at $80 each have $400 cost. Allocating the entire ten-share cost to the half-sale would distort the realized result.

questions.prompt: At the $100 quote, what unrealized gain remains in the unsold five shares?
questions.feedback: The unsold holding is worth $500 and cost $400 before fees. Its $100 gain remains unrealized because those five shares have not been sold.

questions.prompt: At the subsequent $90 quote, what is the remaining marked value?
questions.feedback: Multiply five remaining shares by $90. The new $450 mark changes the unsold position, while the earlier $500 sale receipt remains part of cash.

questions.prompt: At $90, what unrealized gain remains against the unsold shares’ cost?
questions.feedback: Compare $450 current value with $400 remaining cost. There is still a $50 unrealized gain even though the quote fell after the partial sale.

questions.prompt: What is sale cash plus the final unsold holding’s value?
questions.feedback: Add the earlier $500 gross sale receipt to $450 remaining marked value. Compare this $950 combined amount with the original $800 total cost.

questions.prompt: What is total gross gain across sold and unsold shares at the end?
questions.feedback: The $100 realized gain and $50 remaining unrealized gain total $150. The same result follows from $950 combined value minus $800 original cost.

questions.prompt: Which part of the $500 sale receipt is recovered original cost?
questions.feedback: The five sold shares originally cost $400. Only the remaining $100 is gross realized gain; the full cash receipt includes returned investment principal.

rows.title: The quote changes before you submit

questions.prompt: What is the two-unit notional using the later quote?
questions.feedback: Multiply two units by the later $510 quote. The notional becomes $1,020, $20 more than the earlier estimate. The relevant input must be identified before judging the debit.

questions.prompt: What is the later total debit including the stated fee?
questions.feedback: The fee is $1,020 × 0.001 = $1.02. Add it to notional for a $1,021.02 debit. A fee calculated on the earlier estimate would not match this assumed transaction.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful review step after a changed quote?
options: Assume the provider owes the earlier price
Treat the difference as proof of manipulation
Compare the submitted trade record with the earlier estimate
questions.feedback: The record and timestamps can explain whether different inputs were used. A discrepancy deserves investigation, but it does not independently prove wrongdoing. A periodic quote is not a promise of a future real-market fill.

questions.prompt: What notional was expected when two units were first estimated at $500?
questions.feedback: Two units times the original $500 quote gives $1,000 notional. That estimate changes when the quote used for the later calculation changes.

questions.prompt: What fee was expected on the original $1,000 notional?
questions.feedback: Applying 0.1% to $1,000 gives $1. The initial estimated total debit was therefore $1,001 rather than exactly the notional.

questions.prompt: How much larger is the revised total debit than the original $1,001 estimate?
questions.feedback: The later debit is $1,021.02. Subtract the original $1,001 estimate to get $20.02, including both the notional difference and its fee effect.

questions.prompt: What percentage increase occurred in the quote from $500 to $510?
questions.feedback: Divide the $10 quote increase by the original $500. This 2% quote move also raises two-unit notional by 2% before fees.

questions.prompt: In the separate $490 quote branch, what is the two-unit notional?
questions.feedback: Multiply two units by $490 to obtain $980. This alternative branch uses its own stated quote rather than the $510 quote from the first continuation.

questions.prompt: What total debit applies in that $490 branch?
questions.feedback: The $980 notional incurs a $0.98 fee at 0.1%. Add the purchase notional and charge to get $980.98 total cash debit.

questions.prompt: Which record distinguishes a displayed estimate from an executed order?
options: Only the latest chart colour
The execution receipt’s quantity, price, fee and time
Only the older screenshot of the quote
questions.feedback: A displayed estimate can become outdated before submission. The completed order receipt identifies the actual inputs and charge used by the transaction.

rows.title: A closed market can have a fresh fetch

questions.prompt: Does a Sunday fetch prove the stock traded on Sunday?
options: Yes; all markets share crypto hours
No; it may return the earlier observation
Yes; every fetch creates a market trade
questions.feedback: Fetching data and observing a new market transaction are different events. The case explicitly supplies an earlier stock observation; a recent HTTP response must not be presented as evidence of Sunday stock trading.

questions.prompt: Should the stock inherit the crypto quote’s freshness label?
options: Yes; one fresh quote refreshes all holdings
No; freshness belongs to each observation
Yes; both are on one page
questions.feedback: Each asset has its own source and timestamp. A shared page or batch request does not make every observation equally recent. Per-asset freshness prevents a current crypto quote from hiding an older stock mark.

questions.prompt: What wording best describes this stock mark?
options: A guaranteed Sunday sale price
Last observed quote, with its Friday timestamp
Live Sunday stock tick
questions.feedback: The supplied timestamp gives readers evidence for the mark’s age. “Last observed” is precise without inventing a new transaction or promising an executable price during a different market session.

questions.prompt: How many hours old is the stock observation at the Sunday fetch?
options: 48 hours
24 hours
Zero hours
questions.feedback: Friday 16:00 to Sunday 16:00 spans two days, or 48 hours in this fixed-time worksheet. The fetch timestamp does not replace the observation timestamp.

questions.prompt: How old is the crypto observation at Sunday 16:00?
options: 48 hours
Zero minutes
Two minutes
questions.feedback: Subtract Sunday 15:58 from 16:00 to obtain two minutes. That age belongs to the crypto quote and cannot be assigned to the stock.

questions.prompt: Which phrase would misrepresent the stock data in this case?
options: Cached eligible stock mark
Stock price newly observed on Sunday at 16:00
Stock observation from Friday, retrieved Sunday
questions.feedback: No new stock observation is supplied on Sunday. Calling the mark newly observed would confuse a successful retrieval with the underlying market event.

questions.prompt: Does a 48-hour-old mark establish the stock’s next reopening price?
options: No; the reopening price is not supplied
Yes; a cached quote guarantees the next trade
Yes; the page fetch locks the stock price
questions.feedback: The prior eligible mark can support a labelled valuation, but it does not predict or guarantee the price at the next trading session.

questions.prompt: What extra information could affect whether Friday is the last eligible observation?
options: Only the crypto refresh rate
Only the browser’s battery level
The venue’s actual trading-session calendar and source rules
questions.feedback: Trading calendars and provider coverage determine which observations are eligible. The worksheet’s simplified timing should not be converted into a universal venue rule.

questions.prompt: Which timestamp may legitimately change on a Sunday cache retrieval?
options: The original stock trade date
The page’s fetch time
The original stock observation time
questions.feedback: A retrieval creates a new fetch timestamp. Preserving the older observation allows the interface to show the mark’s real age rather than falsely making it fresh.

questions.prompt: What is a defensible combined-account freshness description?
options: Mixed ages, with each holding’s observation shown
Every holding is real-time because one is recent
All assets share the newest crypto timestamp
questions.feedback: Different holdings can depend on different observation windows. Showing their individual ages avoids treating one fresh asset as evidence that the entire account has current prices.

rows.title: A high win rate can lose money

questions.prompt: What is the total from the eight winners?
questions.feedback: Eight gains of $10 sum to $80. A count of profitable attempts does not tell you the total dollars earned unless the size of each outcome is included.

questions.prompt: What is the net result across all ten attempts?
questions.feedback: The two $60 losses total $120. Subtract $120 from $80 for a $40 loss. The 80% win rate is accurate, but it does not make the sample profitable.

questions.prompt: Which summary better explains performance than win rate alone?
options: Win frequency plus gain/loss sizes and costs
Only the largest winning streak
Only the number of green entries
questions.feedback: Frequency and magnitude must be considered together. Costs can further reduce net results. A useful review includes all outcomes rather than selecting a statistic that looks favorable while omitting the account impact.

questions.prompt: What dollar loss comes from the two original $60 losers?
questions.feedback: Two losing attempts at $60 each produce $120 in losses. Comparing this amount with $80 total winnings reveals why the high win rate is insufficient.

questions.prompt: What is average gross result per attempt in the original sample?
questions.feedback: The original sample loses $40 across ten attempts. Dividing by ten gives a −$4 average gross result, despite eight wins.

questions.prompt: What is the original average winner-to-loser magnitude ratio?
questions.feedback: A typical winner is $10 while a loser is $60. The 1:6 payoff-size ratio differs from the 8:2 count of winning and losing attempts.

questions.prompt: With two $30 losses instead, what is the alternative gross result?
questions.feedback: The eight winners still total $80, but the alternative losses total $60. Subtract losses to obtain a $20 gross gain at the same 80% win rate.

questions.prompt: What total cost applies at $1 per attempt in either ten-attempt sample?
questions.feedback: Charge the stated $1 for every attempt, including losses. Ten attempts therefore cost $10; counting only the eight winners would miss two charges.

questions.prompt: What is the alternative sample’s net result after those costs?
questions.feedback: Reduce its $20 gross gain by $10 costs. The sample remains positive, but its net result is smaller than the headline price-only result.

questions.prompt: Which factor changed performance while leaving the win rate unchanged?
options: The number of winning attempts
The percentage of winners
The average losing amount
questions.feedback: Both samples have eight wins and two losses. Reducing loser size changes net dollars even with an identical win-rate summary.

rows.title: One rumor is not three independent sources

questions.prompt: How many original rumor sources are stated here?
options: Three
Four
One
questions.feedback: The three posts share one anonymous origin. Multiple repetitions can amplify visibility without adding independent evidence. The source chain matters more than the raw number of posts.

questions.prompt: What would be a stronger next verification step?
options: Count more reposts of the same rumor
Assume popularity confirms accuracy
Find a relevant primary statement or filing
questions.feedback: A primary record can provide attributable information to compare with the claim. It may confirm, contradict or leave the rumor unresolved. More copies of the same unsupported statement do not independently verify it.

questions.prompt: How should the claim be labelled while unresolved?
options: A confirmed company fact
A guaranteed catalyst
An unverified rumor with its source identified
questions.feedback: Labelling the uncertainty prevents an unattributed claim from being presented as established evidence. A price reaction or a large audience does not itself prove that the underlying statement is correct.

questions.prompt: How many independent stated rumor origins are there after the fourth repost?
options: Two
One
Four
questions.feedback: The fourth message still traces to the same anonymous origin. Repost count increases distribution without adding a new independent source for the claim.

questions.prompt: What does a company document silent on the rumor establish?
options: It does not by itself confirm or disprove the rumor
It automatically proves the rumor true
It proves every anonymous claim false
questions.feedback: A document that does not address the claim supplies no direct resolution. Its primary-source status does not make unrelated silence into confirmation.

questions.prompt: Which finding would directly improve verification of the specific claim?
options: A fifth repost of the same anonymous text
More reactions on the first post
Relevant attributable evidence addressing the allegation
questions.feedback: Verification improves when evidence addresses the actual allegation and can be traced to an accountable source. Popularity and repetition do not provide that link.

questions.prompt: Why is three reposts not equivalent to three independent confirmations?
options: Only the first person can ever publish evidence
They share the same underlying source
All reposts are necessarily false
questions.feedback: Dependence matters: the messages reproduce one origin rather than three separate observations. This does not prove falsity, but it prevents treating the count as corroboration.

questions.prompt: How should a unresolved claim appear in a practice journal?
options: Attributed and explicitly unverified
Presented as a confirmed company event
Removed from uncertainty notes because it is popular
questions.feedback: Attribution and an unresolved label preserve the difference between a claim and established information. That helps future review avoid treating repeated rumor as fact.

questions.prompt: Does the rumor’s popularity supply a probability of its truth in this case?
options: Yes; three shares imply 75% truth
Yes; more shares guarantee accuracy
No; no calibrated reliability evidence was given
questions.feedback: The supplied repost count has no calibrated relationship to truth. A probability would need a defensible method and relevant evidence beyond social repetition.

questions.prompt: Which source-note structure best preserves this chain?
options: Only the most-liked message saved
Origin, repost links and verification status recorded separately
Every repost labelled an independent original
questions.feedback: Keeping origin and distribution distinct exposes dependencies. Recording verification status also prevents later readers from assuming an unresolved claim was checked successfully.

rows.title: A rebound that does not restore the balance

questions.prompt: What balance follows the 20% rebound from $80,000?
questions.feedback: The rebound adds $80,000 × 0.20 = $16,000. The resulting $96,000 is still $4,000 below the initial balance. The rise and fall use different dollar bases.

questions.prompt: What percentage gain from $80,000 would restore $100,000?
questions.feedback: The missing $20,000 must be divided by the current $80,000: 0.25. A 25% rise recovers the original balance. This arithmetic says nothing about how likely or how soon such a rise is.

questions.prompt: What is the full-period return after the stated rebound?
questions.feedback: Compare the final $96,000 with the original $100,000. The $4,000 shortfall is 4% of starting value. Compounding multiplies interval growth factors; adding the two percentages would give the wrong answer.

questions.prompt: How many dollars were lost in the initial fall?
questions.feedback: Subtract the $80,000 trough from the $100,000 start. This $20,000 loss represents 20% of starting equity, rather than 20% of the later trough.

questions.prompt: How many dollars were gained in the stated 20% rebound?
questions.feedback: Multiply the reduced $80,000 balance by 20%. The $16,000 gain is smaller than the earlier loss even though the interval percentages have the same magnitude.

questions.prompt: How far below the original start is the $96,000 account?
questions.feedback: Subtract current $96,000 from original $100,000. The $4,000 remaining gap is distinct from both the $20,000 first loss and $16,000 rebound gain.

questions.prompt: What rise from $96,000 would exactly restore the start, approximately?
questions.feedback: Divide the required $4,000 recovery by current $96,000 equity. Using the original balance as denominator would understate the next interval’s required return.

questions.prompt: In the separate 5% gain branch, what is the next balance?
questions.feedback: Multiplying $96,000 by 1.05 gives $100,800. This branch goes $800 above the original account balance; the gain is calculated from its own interval start.

questions.prompt: In the separate 5% loss branch, what is the next balance?
questions.feedback: Multiply $96,000 by 0.95 to get $91,200. The $4,800 interval loss should not be calculated from the original $100,000 account instead.

questions.prompt: Why can a profitable interval still leave recovery incomplete?
options: Recovery uses only the count of winning days
Equity may remain below the original reference balance
Every gain erases all previous losses
questions.feedback: An interval can be positive while equity remains below its starting level or peak. Recovery requires comparing actual balances with an explicitly chosen reference.

rows.title: A spread is not a commission

questions.prompt: At which stated quote does this hypothetical buyer purchase?
options: $100 midpoint
$101 ask
$99 bid
questions.feedback: A buyer accepting the displayed seller’s price crosses the ask at $101. The midpoint is a comparison reference, not a guaranteed executable quote in this example.

questions.prompt: What happens after immediately selling at the unchanged bid?
options: A $2 gross gain
A $2 gross loss
No loss because the midpoint is stable
questions.feedback: Paying $101 and receiving $99 produces a $2 loss before commissions. An unchanged midpoint does not remove the difference between the two sides of the market.

questions.prompt: How should this worksheet be compared with TradeHQ?
options: As the simulator’s hidden $2 fee
As a separate execution-cost concept
As proof TradeHQ fills at a real exchange ask
questions.feedback: This exercise describes an explicitly hypothetical bid-ask venue. The simulator uses marked snapshots and its stated fee; a lesson must not invent exchange routing, order-book fills or costs that the product does not implement.

questions.prompt: What is the dollar width between the stated bid and ask?
options: $2 per unit
$1 per unit
$200 per unit
questions.feedback: Subtract $99 bid from $101 ask to obtain a $2 spread. The midpoint is between the two quotes but does not reduce their actual separation.

questions.prompt: What is the arithmetic midpoint of the bid and ask?
questions.feedback: Average $99 and $101 to get $100. A reference midpoint is not proof that either crossing transaction in this worksheet executes at that value.

questions.prompt: What does buying ten units at the ask cost before commissions?
questions.feedback: Ten units at the $101 ask require $1,010. Using the midpoint instead would understate the explicit buy price supplied by the case.

questions.prompt: What proceeds come from selling those ten units immediately at the bid?
questions.feedback: Ten units at the unchanged $99 bid yield $990 before commissions. The proceeds use the buyer’s available bid, not the earlier ask.

questions.prompt: What is the ten-unit round-trip loss with quotes unchanged?
questions.feedback: Subtract $990 sale proceeds from $1,010 purchase cost. The $20 difference is ten times the $2 per-unit spread, even without commissions.

questions.prompt: What is that loss as a percentage of the $1,010 buy cost, approximately?
questions.feedback: Divide the $20 loss by $1,010 cash spent. A percentage using the bid proceeds as denominator answers a different question and gives a different result.

questions.prompt: Would a separate commission eliminate the spread cost?
options: No; it would be an additional cost under its own rule
Yes; commission replaces the bid-ask difference
Yes; the midpoint refunds every spread
questions.feedback: A commission and spread arise from different mechanisms. If both apply, calculate each explicitly rather than treating one as compensation for the other.

rows.title: A ticker can identify more than one asset

questions.prompt: What is the value of ten units of project A at its stated quote?
questions.feedback: Ten units multiplied by project A’s $2 quote give $20. Using the other project’s $20 quote would value the holding at $200 and introduce a tenfold identity error.

questions.prompt: Which field helps distinguish the two listings?
options: The explicit provider asset identifier
Only the shared ticker
The higher price
questions.feedback: A short symbol can be ambiguous. A stable provider identifier and project information help establish which asset is meant. Price magnitude is not a dependable way to resolve an identity mismatch.

questions.prompt: What should happen when an asset mapping is uncertain?
options: Flag it instead of silently using another project
Use the first symbol match
Average the unrelated project prices
questions.feedback: A wrong identity makes subsequent calculations misleading even if multiplication is correct. Flagging an unsupported or uncertain mapping is more honest than silently substituting a different asset with a familiar symbol.

questions.prompt: What value would the incorrect B quote assign to ten A units?
questions.feedback: Ten units times the incorrect $20 quote gives $200. The arithmetic is internally consistent, but the instrument identity feeding it is wrong.

questions.prompt: By how many dollars does that incorrect mark overstate the holding?
questions.feedback: The correct A value is $20 and the incorrect value is $200. Subtract to obtain a $180 overstatement caused by the mapping, not market performance.

questions.prompt: How many times as large is the erroneous mark as the correct mark?
options: Ten times
Two times
One hundred times
questions.feedback: Divide the incorrect $200 mark by the correct $20 value. A shared ticker led to a tenfold valuation error in the selected example.

questions.prompt: What should a repaired mapping preserve about the original holding?
options: It becomes ten units of B automatically
It becomes one unit of B to match dollars
It remains ten units of project A
questions.feedback: Repairing a quote lookup should not change the owned instrument or quantity. The account bought A, so corrections must restore A’s appropriate mark.

questions.prompt: Which information provides stronger identity evidence than the short ticker?
options: Only a similar logo colour
Provider ID and project or contract details
Only a matching first letter
questions.feedback: A unique provider identifier and project details help disambiguate reused symbols. A ticker or appearance alone cannot establish the instrument being valued.

questions.prompt: Should a lookup uncertainty be represented as a verified current quote?
options: No; expose the uncertainty and use a labelled fallback if needed
Yes; the higher price is safer
Yes; any matching symbol is sufficient
questions.feedback: Uncertain identity prevents a defensible provider mark. A clearly labelled fallback preserves the distinction between missing mapping evidence and a verified price.

questions.prompt: Which audit would reveal this identity error most directly?
options: Count how many times the page refreshed
Check whether both numbers are positive
Compare the holding’s identifier with the fetched quote’s identifier
questions.feedback: A positive numeric response can still describe the wrong asset. Matching identifiers across the holding and quote is necessary before validating the valuation arithmetic.

rows.title: A few winners do not establish an edge

questions.prompt: What is the observed win rate for the three recorded attempts?
options: Proof of a guaranteed 100% future rate
100% within this sample
questions.feedback: Three winners divided by three recorded attempts is 100%. The qualifier matters: it describes these observations only. A tiny observed sample should not be treated as a promise about future outcomes.

questions.prompt: What missing information most affects the claim?
options: A more impressive strategy name
The author’s preferred chart theme
A complete, larger record with losses and selection rules
questions.feedback: You need to know what was counted, whether failed attempts were omitted and how results behave across more conditions. Three selected winners alone cannot separate skill, chance and reporting bias.

questions.prompt: What is an appropriate next practice step?
options: Increase exposure because losses are impossible
Delete any later losing entry
Record prospective attempts under consistent rules
questions.feedback: Define the method before observing results and record subsequent outcomes consistently. That reduces hindsight editing and cherry-picking. Practice remains simulated, and a broader record still carries uncertainty rather than a guarantee.

questions.prompt: What total gross gain was recorded in the first three attempts?
questions.feedback: Three wins at $20 each give $60 total gross gain. This statement describes the supplied observations and does not establish future payoff reliability.

questions.prompt: After adding one losing attempt, what is the expanded observed win rate?
questions.feedback: Three wins out of four total attempts produce 75%. A single added result changes the small-sample rate substantially without changing the first three records.

questions.prompt: What is net gross result across the three wins and one $80 loss?
questions.feedback: Subtract the $80 fourth-attempt loss from $60 earlier gains. The expanded sample loses $20 despite winning on three of four attempts.

questions.prompt: What is the expanded average gross result per attempt?
questions.feedback: Divide the $20 sample loss by four attempts. The −$5 average reflects payoff sizes as well as the counts of wins and losses.

questions.prompt: Would hiding the fourth attempt make the method’s reported evidence representative?
options: No; it would select only favourable observations
Yes; losing attempts do not count
Yes; the original headline must stay unchanged
questions.feedback: A transparent record includes the fourth result under the same inclusion rule. Removing it after seeing the outcome would introduce selection bias.

questions.prompt: Does the fourth attempt prove every future attempt will lose?
options: Yes; one loss guarantees a permanent negative edge
Yes; the first three wins become invalid
No; the expanded sample is still small
questions.feedback: The added loss weakens the initial success claim but does not establish all future outcomes. Keep uncertainty explicit and avoid reversing one absolute claim into another.

questions.prompt: What review would provide stronger evidence than either short headline?
options: A promise to ignore future losses
A defined inclusion rule, more observations and costs/exposure records
Only more screenshots of wins
questions.feedback: Broader consistently recorded evidence supports better assessment of repeatability. Costs, exposure and predetermined inclusion rules matter alongside the number of observations.

rows.title: Paper results omit some real-money pressures

questions.prompt: What is the paper account’s stated return?
questions.feedback: The hypothetical gain is $10,000 on $100,000, or 10%. It is a virtual result under the simulator’s inputs and rules, not evidence that real money has been earned.

questions.prompt: What does this result fail to establish?
options: Whether virtual positions were displayed
The same real-world outcome under different constraints
Whether subtraction is possible
questions.feedback: The experiment does not reproduce every real cost, fill condition, emotional pressure or personal constraint. A paper gain can support learning while remaining insufficient to predict real returns.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful description of the achievement?
options: Proof that losses are no longer possible
A simulated result with a reviewable process and limitations
A certified real-money profit
questions.feedback: Report the virtual outcome, the assumptions and the record of decisions. This preserves the educational value without turning one simulation into a guarantee or a certification of trading skill.

questions.prompt: How many virtual dollars did the stated paper balance gain?
questions.feedback: Subtract $100,000 starting virtual equity from $110,000 ending equity. The gain is a simulator result, rather than cash earned in a real account.

questions.prompt: Does this virtual result create $10,000 that can be withdrawn as real money?
options: Yes; a profitable practice trade creates withdrawable cash
Yes; completing the course redeems it
No; the balance is virtual
questions.feedback: TradeHQ’s paper holdings and cash are educational simulation records. Their returns do not create real funds or establish a withdrawable financial entitlement.

questions.prompt: In the separate $1,500-extra-cost worksheet, what gain remains?
questions.feedback: Subtract the stipulated $1,500 additional cost from the $10,000 gross result. This arithmetic illustrates cost sensitivity without estimating actual execution expenses.

questions.prompt: What return would that $8,500 gain represent on $100,000, before other differences?
questions.feedback: Divide the hypothetical $8,500 gain by the $100,000 reference capital. This alternative return reflects a chosen cost assumption, not a proven real-money outcome.

questions.prompt: Which real-money constraint was not tested by the virtual starting balance alone?
options: The written arithmetic of subtracting balances
Whether virtual cash is labelled virtual
The user’s actual liquidity needs and ability to bear loss
questions.feedback: A virtual account does not reproduce the user’s real savings needs or personal loss constraints. Those factors cannot be inferred from a profitable simulated record.

questions.prompt: Could real-money emotions differ despite identical written trade rules?
options: No; a streak badge fixes all reactions
Yes; financial stakes can change behaviour
No; paper gains guarantee identical behaviour
